specPoints.text: CORE PRACTICAL 7 The oxidation of propan-1-ol to produce propanal and propanoic acid. Further suggested practical: Investigation of reactions of primary and secondary alcohols, including propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol

primer.text: One alcohol, two destinations. This core practical drips propan-1-ol into cooled acidified dichromate, distilling propanal before it over-oxidises or refluxing to propanoic acid, then closes with the hazard ledger: flammable alcohols, an oxidising reagent, and the precautions that keep both tame.

lessons.title: Core Practical 7: from propan-1-ol to propanal and beyond
sourceHeadings: Synthesis and purification of propanal and propanoic acid
lessons.opening: This core practical turns propan-1-ol into propanal, or all the way to propanoic acid, using acidified dichromate. The technique controls how far the oxidation climbs: dropwise addition into cooled oxidant, reflux for the acid, or distillation for the aldehyde, followed by purification.
keyPoints: Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes, which oxidise further to carboxylic acids; propan-1-ol gives propanal then propanoic acid.
20 cm3 of acidified potassium dichromate solution is cooled in an iced water bath inside a 50 cm3 pear-shaped flask.
Anti-bumping granules are added, and 1 cm3 of propan-1-ol is dripped slowly into the reflux condenser by pipette.
After warming to room temperature the mixture is heated for 20 minutes by electric heater or water bath, never a naked flame.
The product is purified by distillation, collecting the propanal fraction, or refluxed with excess oxidant for the acid.

low.restatement: Cool the oxidant, drip the alcohol in slowly, then heat without flames: distil promptly for the aldehyde or keep refluxing with excess oxidant for the acid, purifying the product afterwards by distillation.
low.analogy: A climbing route with a mid-station: leave the train at propanal by distilling early, or ride on to propanoic acid by staying in the reflux carriage.
low.examPointer: Quote the dropwise addition, the iced bath and the flame-free heating as the three control measures in practical-plan answers.

medium.restatement: The dropwise addition into cooled dichromate keeps the alcohol's residence time short so the aldehyde stage is caught; continuing to reflux hands the aldehyde more contact with the oxidant, driving it to the acid; distillation then separates whichever product was targeted by its boiling point.
medium.analogy: A conveyor belt: short rides stop at the first station (propanal), long rides continue to the terminal (propanoic acid).
medium.examPointer: Explain why the ice bath matters - the exothermic oxidation and volatile alcohol both demand temperature control from the start.

check.stem: Why is the propan-1-ol added drop by drop into the cooled oxidising agent?

options.text: To control the exothermic oxidation and limit the alcohol's exposure, catching the aldehyde stage
options.explanation: Slow addition plus cooling keeps the reaction manageable and stops short where intended.

options.text: Because the alcohol is too viscous to pour
options.explanation: Propan-1-ol is a thin liquid; a pipette serves precision, not viscosity.
The iced bath cools; the dropwise rate controls exposure.

options.text: Because the full volume reacts explosively
options.explanation: With control the reaction is safe; portioning is precaution, not desperation.

check.stem: Heating is done with an electric heater or water bath rather than a Bunsen burner because

options.text: Propan-1-ol is flammable, and naked flames ignite its vapours
options.explanation: The flame-free heating is a direct fire-safety measure.
Bunsens heat glass routinely.
The heater supplies heat only.
Water baths here are set to warm, not cool.

check.stem: Oxidising propan-1-ol all the way to propanoic acid requires

options.text: Refluxing with excess acidified dichromate so the aldehyde is re-oxidised
options.explanation: Extended contact with excess oxidant drives the second oxidation stage.

options.text: Distilling the aldehyde the moment it forms
options.explanation: That deliberately stops at propanal.
More substrate does not advance oxidation; more oxidant contact does.
Reduction runs the opposite direction of the intended oxidation.

check.stem: The product propanal is purified by

options.text: Distillation, collecting the fraction at propanal's boiling point
options.explanation: The volatile aldehyde distils ahead of higher-boiling species.
Filtration removes solids; the products are liquids.
Titration measures concentration, not purification.
Flame tests identify metal ions.

check.stem: Anti-bumping granules are placed in the pear-shaped flask to

options.text: Promote smooth boiling during the heating stage
options.explanation: The granules provide nucleation sites that prevent violent bumping.
The granules are chemically inert.

options.text: Absorb the propanal as it forms
options.explanation: Absorption would destroy the product; the granules do not absorb.
No filtration happens in the flask.

check.stem: Name the two organic products obtainable from oxidising propan-1-ol.
check.modelAnswer: Propanal, the aldehyde, and propanoic acid, the carboxylic acid formed on further oxidation.

check.stem: State the safety precautions attached to the heating stage.
check.modelAnswer: Use an electric heater or water bath instead of a naked flame, because propan-1-ol is flammable, and keep the flask cooled during the addition.

check.stem: Explain why the pear-shaped flask is cooled in an iced water bath before the alcohol is added.
check.modelAnswer: The oxidation is exothermic and the alcohol is volatile, so starting cold absorbs the reaction's heat release and prevents uncontrolled boiling or vapour loss during the dropwise addition.

check.stem: A student distils the reaction mixture and collects a fraction that gives a positive Tollens' test. Identify the fraction and state the apparatus change that would instead have delivered propanoic acid.
check.modelAnswer: The Tollens-positive fraction is propanal, the aldehyde; obtaining the acid instead requires the reflux set-up with excess oxidant, retaining everything in the flask rather than distilling early.

lessons.title: Hazards in the oxidation laboratory
lessons.opening: Every reagent in this practical carries a warning label. The alcohols are flammable and harmful, the dichromate is a strong oxidising agent, and the routine answers are fume cupboards, water-mopping of spillages and distance from naked flames.
keyPoints: The alcohols used, such as propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol and pentan-1-ol, are flammable and often harmful to health.
Alcohols must be kept away from naked flames such as Bunsen burners.
Skin contact and inhalation of vapour should be avoided, with a fume cupboard used for harmful alcohols.
Potassium dichromate is a strong oxidising agent requiring careful handling.
Spillages should be mopped up immediately with plenty of water.

low.restatement: Match each hazard to its control: flames off for flammable alcohols, fume cupboard for harmful vapours, careful handling and water mopping for the oxidising dichromate.
low.analogy: A fire triangle map: remove the ignition source, contain the vapour, and wash away the spill before any of them meet.
low.examPointer: In risk-assessment answers pair every named reagent with its specific precaution rather than a generic 'be careful'.

medium.restatement: The hazard logic chains: volatile flammable alcohols need an ignition-free heating route and vapour control; a strong oxidant like dichromate intensifies any fire it meets, so it is stored and handled away from combustibles, and spillages are diluted fast to defuse both hazards at once.
medium.analogy: Keeping matches away from petrol cans, with a hose ready: the same separation and response logic runs this bench.
medium.examPointer: Justify the water-mopping response as dilution of both a flammable vapour source and an oxidising concentrate.

check.stem: Why must propan-1-ol be kept away from naked flames?

options.text: Its vapour is flammable and ignites readily at a flame
options.explanation: A Bunsen burner near the alcohol risks immediate fire.

options.text: The flame would boil the alcohol instantly
options.explanation: Boiling is controllable; ignition is the hazard.

options.text: The flame oxidises the alcohol dangerously
options.explanation: The dichromate does the oxidation; the flame's hazard is ignition.

options.text: The alcohol is corrosive to burners
options.explanation: Corrosion is not the concern.

check.stem: Potassium dichromate requires careful handling because it is

options.explanation: The oxidising power is the declared hazard requiring care.
Dichromate is an oxidising solid in solution, not a fuel.
Category nonsense; it is an ionic solid.
It oxidises alcohols precisely because it is an oxidant.

check.stem: Spillages of the reagents are dealt with by

options.text: Mopping up right away with plenty of water
options.explanation: Dilution removes both the flammable vapour source and the oxidising concentrate.
Evaporation spreads the flammable vapour hazard.
Igniting a flammable spill is the opposite of safe.

options.text: Sweeping them into the bin dry
options.explanation: Dry disposal preserves both hazards.

check.stem: A fume cupboard is used for harmful alcohols because

options.text: Their harmful vapours must be drawn away from the chemist's breathing zone
options.explanation: The extract removes inhalation exposure at its source.

options.text: The alcohols react with laboratory air violently
options.explanation: No such violent reaction occurs.
The cupboard's role is extraction, not cooling.
Solubility is unaffected by the cupboard.

check.stem: Which set of alcohols does the practical name as flammable and harmful?

options.explanation: The named three all carry the flammable and harmful labels.
Water is not flammable; the named set is different.
That pair is not the practical's named set.
The label contradicts that claim directly.

check.stem: State the two personal-protection measures attached to the harmful alcohols.
check.modelAnswer: Avoid contact with skin and avoid breathing the vapour, using a fume cupboard where needed.

check.stem: State the handling rule for potassium dichromate in this practical.
check.modelAnswer: Its declared hazard is oxidising strength, so it is handled deliberately, and spillages are mopped at once with plenty of water.

check.stem: Explain why diluting spillages with water reduces both the fire and the oxidising hazards.
check.modelAnswer: Water dilutes the alcohol below its flammable vapour range and spreads the dichromate out of its concentrated oxidising state, so one response defuses the two separate hazards simultaneously.

check.stem: During the practical, a few millilitres of propan-1-ol spill near a lit Bunsen burner. State the immediate actions in order and the reason for each.
check.modelAnswer: Extinguish the burner first to remove the ignition source, then mop the spill with plenty of water to dilute the flammable liquid, and ventilate or use the fume cupboard to clear harmful vapour.

glossary.definition: The aldehyde from oxidising propan-1-ol once, boiling lower than its parent alcohol.
The carboxylic acid from oxidising propanal further under reflux with excess oxidant.
Inert granules that give nucleation sites for smooth boiling in heated flasks.
